but i say unto you, that ye resist not evil: but whosoever shall smite thee on thy right cheek, turn to him the other also.

and if any man will sue thee at the law, and take away thy coat, let him have thy cloke also.

and whosoever shall compel thee to go a mile, go with him twain.

give to him that asketh thee, and from him that would borrow of thee turn not thou away.

ye have heard that it hath been said, thou shalt love thy neighbour, and hate thine enemy.

but i say unto you, love your enemies, bless them that curse you, do good to them that hate you, and pray for them which despitefully use you, and persecute you;

that ye may be the children of your father which is in heaven: for he maketh his sun to rise on the evil and on the good, and sendeth rain on the just and on the unjust.

for if ye love them which love you, what reward have ye? do not even the publicans the same?

and if ye salute your brethren only, what do ye more than others? do not even the publicans so?

be ye therefore perfect, even as your father which is in heaven is perfect. the didache is an early christian teaching text whose opening presents life as a choice between two ways. its way of life begins with love of god and neighbor. the contrast is developed through speech, generosity, sexual conduct, the protection of life, and treatment of enemies. the text joins love for the creator and neighbor with restraint from doing to others what one would reject for oneself. it then describes love of enemies, nonretaliation, and giving. its account also distinguishes genuine need from the wrongful taking of support, so the teaching includes responsibility in both giving and receiving. the next selection names killing, sexual wrongdoing, theft, false witness, magic, greed, and hypocrisy among the actions rejected. it also connects truthful speech with conduct that fulfills what is said. these prohibitions give concrete content to the contrast between the two ways.

the didache on conduct and generosity the didache: life, initiation, and thanksgiving mercy almsgiving anger other sins forbidden. 1. my child,  flee from every evil thing, and from every likeness of it. 2. be not prone to anger, for anger leadeth the way to murder; neither jealous, nor quarrelsome, nor of hot temper; for out of all these murders are engendered. 3. my child, be not a lustful one; for lust leadeth the way to fornication; neither a filthy talker, nor of lofty eye; for out of all these adulteries are engendered. 4. my child, be not an observer of omens, since it leadeth the way to idolatry; neither an enchanter, nor an astrologer, nor a purifier, nor be willing to took at these things; irenaeus on the eucharist and bodily resurrection early church order and the bodily hope body resurrection eucharist when christ visited us in his grace, he did not come to what did not belong to him: also, by shedding his true blood for us, and exhibiting to us his true flesh in the eucharist, he conferred upon our flesh the capacity of salvation. 1. and vain likewise are those who say that god came to those things which did not belong to him, as if covetous of another's property; in order that he might deliver up that man who had been created by another, to that god who had neither made nor formed anything, but who also was deprived from the beginning of his own proper formation of men. the advent, therefore, of him whom these men represent as coming to the things of others, was not righteous; nor did he truly redeem us by his own blood, if he did not really become man, restoring to his own handiwork what was said [of it] in the beginning, that man was made after the image and likeness of god; not snatching away by stratagem the property of another, but taking possession of his own in a righteous and gracious manner. as far as concerned the apostasy, indeed, he redeems us righteously from it by his own blood; but as regards us who have been redeemed, [he does this] graciously. for we have given nothing to him previously, nor does he desire anything from us, as if he stood in need of it; but we do stand in need of fellowship with him. and for this reason it was that he graciously poured himself out, that he might gather us into the bosom of the father.

2. but vain in every respect are they who despise the entire dispensation of god, and disallow the salvation of the flesh, and treat with contempt its regeneration, maintaining that it is not capable of incorruption. but if this indeed do not attain salvation, then neither did the lord redeem us with his blood, nor is the cup of the eucharist the communion of his blood, nor the bread which we break the communion of his body.  for blood can only come from veins and flesh, and whatsoever else makes up the substance of man, such as the word of god was actually made. by his own blood he redeemed us, as also his apostle declares, "in whom we have redemption through his blood, even the remission of sins." book v, chapter ii; opening selection st. irenaeus of lyons irenaeus: against heresies against heresies ante-nicene fathers, vol.1;1885 alexander roberts and william rambaut the power and glory of god shine forth in the weakness of human flesh, as he will render our body a participator of the resurrection and of immortality, although he has formed it from the dust of the earth; he will also bestow upon it the enjoyment of immortality, just as he grants it this short life in common with the soul. 1. the apostle paul has, moreover, in the most lucid manner, pointed out that man has been delivered over to his own infirmity, lest, being uplifted, he might fall away from the truth. thus he says in the second [epistle] to the corinthians: "and lest i should be lifted up by the sublimity of the revelations, there was given unto me a thorn in the flesh, the messenger of satan to buffet me. and upon this i besought the lord three times, that it might depart from me. but he said unto me, my grace is sufficient for thee; for strength is made perfect in weakness. gladly therefore shall i rather glory in infirmities, that the power of christ may dwell in me."  what, therefore? (as some may exclaim:) did the lord wish, in that case, that his apostles should thus undergo buffeting, and that he should endure such infirmity? even so it was; the word says it. for strength is made perfect in weakness, rendering him a better man who by means of his infirmity becomes acquainted with the power of god. for how could a man have learned that he is himself an infirm being, and mortal by nature, but that god is immortal and powerful, unless he had learned by experience what is in both? for there is nothing evil in learning one's infirmities by endurance; yea, rather, it has even the beneficial effect of preventing him from forming an undue opinion of his own nature (non aberrare in natura sua). but the being lifted up against god, and taking his glory to one's self, rendering man ungrateful, has brought much evil upon him. [and thus, i say, man must learn both things by experience], that he may not be destitute of truth and love either towards himself or his creator.  but the experience of both confers upon him the true knowledge as to god and man, and increases his love towards god. now, where there exists an increase of love, there a greater glory is wrought out by the power of god for those who love him.

the spirit itself beareth witness with our spirit, that we are the children of god:

and if children, then heirs; heirs of god, and joint-heirs with christ; if so be that we suffer with him, that we may be also glorified together. irenaeus argues that salvation concerns the human body as well as the soul. incarnation means the word’s real becoming human, and incorruptibility names the life beyond bodily decay that god gives. the eucharist and the experience of human weakness belong to that argument. irenaeus connects christ’s real blood and flesh with redemption and eucharistic communion. he argues that denying the body’s capacity for salvation would undermine those confessions. the creator saves his own creation by grace, rather than taking a humanity made by some other god. the second passage interprets paul’s weakness through god’s sufficient grace and strength. irenaeus explains how awareness of mortality can correct self-exaltation and deepen knowledge of the creator. the contrast concerns the human creature’s dependence and god’s ability to give life.

my mouth shall speak the praise of the lord: and let all flesh bless his holy name for ever and ever. almighty means that god’s rule extends over all things. cyril explains this confession against accounts that divide divine power or restrict it to one part of reality. he also distinguishes god’s patient tolerance of wrongdoing from an inability to overcome it. cyril connects almighty with the preceding confession of one god, the father of the son. the title excludes a limited or divided account of divine power. it is part of the same explanation of the creed’s opening confession. cyril rejects claims that divine providence reaches heaven but leaves the earth outside god’s care. providence means god’s governing care for creation. his appeal to the psalms supports the claim that neither height nor depth removes a place from god’s presence. cyril also rejects assigning the soul and body to different divine rulers. each such ruler would have a restricted domain and therefore could not be almighty. his account attributes authority over the whole human person to the father of jesus christ. cyril explains the continued existence of evil through god’s patience and providence. he denies that it proves a defeat or lack of divine ability. the passage interprets human struggle and eventual judgment within that distinction. cyril describes created things as serving god, but explicitly distinguishes the son and holy spirit from that category. he joins the rule of the father with service through the son and in the spirit. the remaining discussion presents earthly rulers as dependent on power from above.

and the evening and the morning were the third day. cyril distinguishes seeing a created thing from comprehending the invisible creator. incorporeal means not bodily; incomprehensible here means that god’s nature cannot be fully grasped by human understanding. creation can disclose something of god’s power without making the divine nature measurable. cyril distinguishes god himself from the likeness of divine glory described in ezekiel. his argument takes the prophet’s fear as a sign of the limits of human capacity. bodily sight does not give unrestricted access to the divine nature. cyril says the greatness and beauty of created things permit a proportionate awareness of the maker’s power. a larger understanding of creation can enlarge the person’s conception of its creator. this is a real but limited knowledge, rather than full comprehension of god’s nature. cyril uses the difficulty of understanding ezekiel’s heavenly creatures to illustrate a greater limit before god. if even the described throne exceeds the hearer’s grasp, the invisible god cannot be comprehended through the description. praise for visible divine works remains possible within that limit. cyril explains the creed’s creation clause as identifying the father of christ with the maker of the world. he opposes accounts that disparage the creator or place creation under another divine being. the continuity between creation and christian salvation is central to his argument. the final excerpt praises the ordered heavens and the provision of water for the earth. its physical descriptions use the cosmological language of this ancient exposition. the theological purpose is to defend the goodness and wisdom of the world’s creator.

and i will give unto thee the keys of the kingdom of heaven: and whatsoever thou shalt bind on earth shall be bound in heaven: and whatsoever thou shalt loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven.

then charged he his disciples that they should tell no man that he was jesus the christ. cyril explains why the many names applied to christ refer to one subject. jesus, christ, son, lord, shepherd, and door identify the same savior through different aspects of his identity and work. a title can convey a true relation or action without being a literal description of an ordinary physical object. cyril connects belief in the father with belief in his son. he interprets christ’s names door and way through the son’s disclosure of the father. the relation is therefore central to the knowledge of god described in this passage. cyril draws together the father’s declaration about his beloved son and the scriptural language of divine sonship. he presents honoring the son as belonging to worship of the father. his polemical remarks address the opponents of his own argument. the same christ is called door, way, sheep, and shepherd. cyril explains these through access to the father, the saving passion, humanity, and divine care. the names identify different aspects of one person’s work rather than separate beings. cyril relates christ’s anointing to his priestly work, jesus to saving healing, and lord to his natural and eternal authority. his sonship is not treated as a status gained by adoption. the variety of titles still concerns the one lord jesus christ. the passage describes christ as vine, door, high priest, and sacrificial sheep according to the help he gives. high priest names his mediating relation in this account. cyril emphasizes that this varied work does not alter christ’s own nature or the reality of his sonship.

and the shepherds returned, glorifying and praising god for all the things that they had heard and seen, as it was told unto them. incarnation means the eternal word of god truly becoming human. cyril joins christ’s divinity and humanity in his account of salvation, distinguishing the son’s eternal relation to the father from his human birth of the virgin. his argument rejects both a merely apparent humanity and a merely ordinary man later elevated to divine status. cyril reads john’s statements that the word is god and that the word became flesh together. christ is neither an ordinary man who lacks divinity nor god without the humanity assumed for salvation. the physician comparison explains his real participation in the human condition he heals. cyril appeals to isaiah’s announcement of a virgin conceiving emmanuel in his defense of christ’s birth. his question asks how acceptance of that prophecy relates to acceptance of its fulfillment. the surrounding hostile generalizations belong to his ancient polemic, not to this lesson’s description of contemporary people. cyril distinguishes the word becoming human from theories of an apparent birth or an ordinary man advanced into divine status. he identifies the birth as from the virgin and the holy spirit. the subject of that birth is the same pre-existing word. the son’s existence does not begin with the incarnation. cyril distinguishes his eternal begetting from the father from the humanity assumed for human salvation. he then introduces questions about why god came among humanity and how the virgin birth is understood.

then arose peter, and ran unto the sepulchre; and stooping down, he beheld the linen clothes laid by themselves, and departed, wondering in himself at that which was come to pass. cyril explains christ’s resurrection through the scriptural testimony cited by the apostles. resurrection means a real raising after death, and corruption in these passages means bodily decay. his explanation distinguishes the reality of christ’s death from remaining under death’s power. cyril takes the apostolic phrase about resurrection according to the scriptures as a reason to examine earlier testimony. his announced questions concern the time, place, and witnesses connected with the resurrection. he seeks to make the gospel accounts intelligible as part of that scriptural history. cyril gathers passages that he interprets as testimony to christ’s burial. their images include peace, rest, and the lion lying down. his account connects burial with the saving relation between sinners and god before turning specifically to resurrection. cyril reads the psalm’s promise that god’s holy one will not see corruption as a testimony to life after death. he carefully distinguishes not seeing corruption from never dying. the distinction allows him to affirm both christ’s real death and his release from its continuing power.
